messages.subject_clean: No check on the data argument given to inla
messages.body_plain:
Dear Help,

I have stumbled across an interesting feature of INLA.

The inla function needs a data argument but actually if it does not contain the right variables then inla will look for it in the global environment as glm.nb from MASS does for example.

I must say I thought it was quite good for inla to force one to give a data argument. Maybe it could give a warning when the variables for fitting the model are not found in the data given to inla?

Here an example to explain what I mean.

nbVariable <- rnbinom(n1, mu = 10, size = 0.5)
formula <- as.formula(nbVariable ~ 1)
E <- mean(nbVariable)
dataModel <- as.data.frame(rnorm(1))
# INLA fitting
results <- inla(formula,data=dataModel,
                family='nbinomial',E=E)

It works and uses nbVariable from the global environment since dataModel does not provide the right variable.

Of course this
nbVariable <- rnbinom(n1, mu = 10, size = 0.5)
formula <- as.formula(miscellaneous ~ 1)
E <- mean(nbVariable)
dataModel <- as.data.frame(rnorm(1))
# INLA fitting
results <- inla(formula,data=dataModel,
                family='nbinomial',E=E)
does not work since there is no variable called "miscellaneous".

Best wishes

Maëlle.

Hi

having thought of this, I recall we have discussed it internally earlier
as well, and its all about 'design'.

if we have

y = -1
n = -1
r = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y=1, n=1),
         family = "binomial", Ntrials = n)

then inla will use y=1 and n=1 for 'y' and 'n', as it will look in
'data' first.

the issue is what will happen if we refer to a variable not in 'data',
like

YY = -1
r = inla(YY ~ 1, data = data.frame(y=1, n=1),
         family = "binomial", Ntrials = n)

then it will use 'YY=-1' as 'YY' is not in data. Should we give an error
or warning in this case?? packages like 'glm' and 'lm' have this
behaviour (and this behaviour is kind of built into R) hence we do not
break any R 'style' or 'feature'.

would be nice to have a 'strict' mode, like setting an option would
make the above fail or give a warning. I agree. This would detect an
error if all variables was intentially defined by 'data'. I have looked
over the code, and its messy, and to be honest, I do not have full
control over what is going on or how this works.

one way might be to use

inla.strict = function(...)
{
    <<<do something here>>>
    return(inla(...))
}

where the missing code prevents one from assessing variables in unwanted
environments. I cannot see how this is done though...

H

Here is the representation of the model:

y_i ~ Poisson( E_i*exp(eta_i) )

eta_i = 1 + f(cov1) + cov2 + spatial effects

formula=occurrences~f(inla.group(cov1), model="rw2") + cov2 +  f(district_id, model="bym", graph=g)

Following a previous publication, I used the formula below to transform the response (occurrences) into normal and then fitted the model as a gaussian process:

newresponse=log(occurrences/ncells)

The results from this transformed model look way better and make sense based on my hypotheses (see attached transfmod_cov1.pdf). However I am not convinced about the implications of such transformation.The model also requires to remove all districts with zero occurrences, which might carry important information.

Thank you all for your helpful posts.

y_i ~ Poisson( E_i*exp(eta_i) )

eta_i = 1 + f(cov1) + cov2 + spatial effects

Here is the code for inla:

formula=occurrences~f(inla.group(cov1), model="rw2") + cov2 +  f(district_id, model="bym", graph=g)

cheap.mod= inla(formula, data=Data, family="poisson", verbose=TRUE, control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.1, expand.factor.strategy='inla'), control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian", int.strategy="eb"),  E=ncells)

I grouped cov1 to reduce the number of unique values and tried to change the n option in inla.group() but it does not fix the problem.

Following a previous publication, I used the formula below to transform the response (occurrences) into normal and then fitted the model as a gaussian process:

newresponse=log(occurrences/ncells)

The results from this transformed model look way better and make sense based on my hypotheses (see attached transfmod_cov1.pdf). However I am not convinced about the implications of such transformation.The model also requires to remove all districts with zero occurrences, which might carry important information.

Any pointers will be highly appreciated.

messages.subject: mesh boundaries misbehaving
messages.body_plain:
I've been trying to plot predictions from some spatial models (following Elias Krainski's tutorial a lot!), and was getting large interior gaps in the areas I should be plotting. After poking around, I found that the boundary of the region in the inla.mesh object produced by inla.mesh.2d() isn't ordered in the way expected: sometimes it's a series of non-contiguous segments. Here's an example, where most of the interior gets cut out:

library(inla)
library(maps)
library(rgeos)

USmap=map(database="usa", interior=FALSE, resolution=0, regions="main")
USpolygon=Polygon(coords=cbind(rev(USmap$x),rev(USmap$y)))
# Remove intersections in map
bdry=gBuffer(SpatialPolygons(Srl=list(Polygons(srl=list(USpolygon), ID="eek"))), width=0)

region.bdry <- inla.sp2segment(bdry)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=region.bdry, cutoff=0.5, max.edge=c(1, 3), offset=c(1,1))

Boundary=mesh$loc[mesh$segm$int$idx[,2],] # get the boundary of the region

plot(mesh)
polygon(Boundary[,1:2], col=2, lwd=2) # wait, Lake Michigan isn't in my region!?

I could use region.bdry for my analyses, but in practice that's in a function, so it would mean passing it out of the function, which seems pointless if the same information is being passed in the mesh object. So, can anyone suggest a solution to either correctly order the boundary in the mesh, or pass the boundary to inla.mesh.2d() in a way that preserves it?

Bob

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mesh boundaries misbehaving
messages.body_plain:
> Boundary=mesh$loc[mesh$segm$int$idx[,2],] # get the boundary of the region

That way of extracting the boundary will fail in some (many!)
situations, yes, and is not a recommended or supported way to do this.
Please let us know precisely where the tutorial does this, so we can
correct it.

The correct way depends on what you want to do with the boundary.
Plotting is the easiest, described below.

The first step would be to extract the boundary, with locations, using
   bnd <- inla.mesh.boundary(mesh)
which produces a list of one or more boundary segment objects, but
still in unspecified order.
There will be more than one object only if the boundary segments have
more than one "grp" label, which happens when you either specified such
yourself, or built the mesh directly from an inla.mesh.lattice object.

Plotting of the boundary outline can then be done with
   lines(bnd[[1]], add=FALSE)

The package doesn't currently have functions to convert into
SpatialPolygons objects (only the opposite, from SpatialPolygons to
inla.mesh.segment), but I expect to add that in the near future.

To plot a filled polygon of the domain the easiest method is currently
to plot the mesh itself using the rgl package, specifying colours and
which properties to draw:

plot(mesh, ddraw.segments=TRUE, lwd=2,
      draw.edges=FALSE, draw.vertices=FALSE,
      col="gray", rgl=TRUE)

> So, can anyone suggest a solution to either correctly order the boundary
> in the mesh, or pass the boundary to inla.mesh.2d() in a way that
> preserves it?

There is no way to guarantee any particular order in the internal
representation.  The lines.inla.mesh.segment() function does internally
reorder the nodes in order to do the plotting in the correct order, so
if you need to do more than just plot the outline, you could as a
temporary workaround copy that code.

Finn

In your case I see that you were trying to extract the interior
segments, which can be done with
     inter <- inla.mesh.interior(mesh)

However, there is no guarantee that interior segments even form a closed
loop.  In your mesh construction I think it always will, but there is no
strict guarantee, since interior segments can be broken up by other
interior constraints, as well as exterior boundary segments that remove
parts of the initial domain.

However, to simply plot the outline (which is already done by plot(mesh)
by default, so here I show how to override that), do
   plot(mesh, draw.segments=FALSE)
   lines(inter[[1]], col=2, lwd=2)

Since writing plot.inla.mesh, I have found features in R that would
allow drawing filled triangles without using rgl, but since the mesh
does not store the inside/outside information that wouldn't
automatically allow coloring only the interior triangles.

Sure, I know that for Ntrials=1 one cannot estimate overdispersion since the distribution of the data in this case do not depend on the overdispersion parameter of the betabinomial (denoted rho = 1/(alpha + beta +1) in inla).  So, as long as rho is independent of other parameters in the prior (which it is), the posterior for rho should be equal to the prior, and the posterior for other parameters should be identical to the results produced if using a binomial likelihood instead.  So this is why the example results are unexpected also in the degenerate case - the prior for everything else (the regression intercept and slope) are identical in the two cases.

In any case, my main concern was the problem with predicted values becoming numerically equal to 0 or 1 which appears to cause the crash.  This can easily occur if the response is always zero for some level of a factor in the model (or it can occur in less obvious ways involving some linear combination of covariates).  While parameter estimates obtained in such cases not necessarily can be trusted, it may still be of interest to fit an overparameterized model like this, for example, to assess goodness of fit of some simpler model.

> Sure, I know that for Ntrials=1 one cannot estimate overdispersion since the distribution of the data in this case do not depend on the overdispersion parameter of the betabinomial (denoted rho = 1/(alpha + beta +1) in inla).  So, as long as rho is independent of other parameters in the prior (which it is), the posterior for rho should be equal to the prior, and the posterior for other parameters should be identical to the results produced if using a binomial likelihood instead.

No, that reasoning is incorrect. The prior in the betabinomial model is not equivalent to the prior in the binomial model; they imply different data distributions, so the results should not be expected to be the same.

> So this is why the example results are unexpected also in the degenerate case - the prior for everything else (the regression intercept and slope) are identical in the two cases.

But the data likelihoods are different, which will therefore also affect the other posteriors.
The difference in results are entirely expected.

> In any case, my main concern was the problem with predicted values becoming numerically equal to 0 or 1 which appears to cause the crash.  This can easily occur if the response is always zero for some level of a factor in the model (or it can occur in less obvious ways involving some linear combination of covariates).  While parameter estimates obtained in such cases not necessarily can be trusted, it may still be of interest to fit an overparameterized model like this, for example, to assess goodness of fit of some simpler model.

For model+data such that the posterior mode is degenerate, there is a practical limitation to what can reasonably be expected from a general purpose numerical method.  Where you say that the predicted values become equal to 0 or 1, that's due to the linear predictor becoming close to - or + infinity, and handling that cleanly is non-trivial.  Mathematical theory and numerical reality don't always play well together.  Probably the only thing that can be done is to make sure that values are truncated before being fed into the beta-function, and hoping that that doesn't break something else.

Finn L
